youtube.title: Chatbots Are Over. Here's How an AI Agent Actually Works (and Fails).
youtube.description:
What actually happens between 'just handle it' and the result? This video records one real AI agent run, step by step, and turns it into the five moves that make an agent different from a chatbot, then shows where agents still fail by the makers' own numbers.

The run is a coding agent asked to read three official pricing pages and write a table; every tool call, the one page that refused, and the file it wrote are shown as they happened on 2026-09-28. The computer-use score on screen is Anthropic's own for Claude Opus 5.5; OpenAI's own GPT-6 Astra page is linked below. Reports about OpenAI's next assistant are labelled as reports.

Recorded 2026-09-28.

scenes.chapter: What an agent is, in one sentence

data.title: Chatbots are over. Here's how an **agent** actually works
data.subtitle: One real run, five moves, and the tasks that still fail

lines.text: Every AI company is now selling you an agent, and next they want to sell you one that never logs off.
Most explanations stop at: it can use tools. That tells you nothing about what happens after you press enter.
So I gave one agent a boring task and recorded every step. I will show you the five moves that turn a chatbot into an agent.
Plus the tasks that still go wrong, by the makers' own numbers, and what to do about it.

right.heading: An agent
points: A loop: act, look, act again
A rule for when to stop

lines.text: Here is the one-sentence difference. A chatbot turns your text into text and waits. An agent takes a goal and works until it is done.
On the left, a chatbot: text in, text out, one turn, and it touches nothing outside the chat.
On the right, an agent: a goal, tools it can call, a loop of act, look, act again, and a rule for when to stop.
Everything that makes agents useful, and everything that makes them dangerous, lives in that loop.
Goal, tools, loop. If you remember three words from this video, make it those three.
And a fourth if you have room: stop. An agent without a clear stop rule keeps going. That is how you get last week's headlines.

scenes.chapter: A real run, step by step

messages.name: Owner
messages.text: Find three official prices, write a table.

messages.name: Agent
messages.text: I'll fetch each of the three pages.

lines.text: Now the real run. We gave a coding agent a small job with a checkable result: find three official model prices and write a table.
We named the three pages it could read, told it to leave blank any cell it could not read, and never to guess a number.
It answered with its plan in one line: I will fetch each of the three pages. That is move one: the goal becomes a plan.

steps.title: 4 Act on it
steps.detail: Writes the table, blanks the failed one

steps.title: 5 Stop and report
steps.detail: What it did, what it could not

lines.text: Move one, plan. Move two, call a tool: it fetched all three pages we had named.
Move three, observe. Two pages answered with prices. The third refused with a 403 error, access forbidden.
Move four, act on what it saw. It wrote the table and left the failed model's cells blank, exactly as told.
Move five, stop and report: two sentences, what it did and what it could not do. Five turns, twenty two seconds.
Here is the file. Three rows filled, each with the page its numbers came from. One row honest about being empty.
That empty row is the most important thing in the file. An agent that guesses when a page fails is an agent you cannot use.

messages.name: Agent
messages.text: I fetched two pages and wrote their prices.

messages.name: Agent
messages.text: The third page said 403. I left it blank.

lines.text: Then it stopped and reported, in two sentences we had asked for: what it did, and what it could not do.
The second sentence is the one to look for in any agent you use. The page refused, so I left it blank, rather than guessing.
A good agent tells you where it hit a wall. A bad one paints over the wall and hands you a clean looking file.

data.title: The whole run, in numbers
data.source: Recorded 2026-09-28 with two tools allowed: one to fetch pages, one to write files

lines.text: The whole run in numbers: five turns, three pages fetched, one of them refused, one file written, twenty two seconds.
Nothing here is magic. It is a loop that calls tools and looks at what comes back, and you can read every step of it.

data.title: What the run shows
items: Every tool call is visible: you can read the trail
A failure became a blank cell, not an invented number
The receipt is the file, not the chat

lines.text: Three things this small run shows.
First, every tool call is visible. Agents leave a trail, and you can read it.
Second, a failure became a blank cell, not an invented number, because we said so up front.
Third, the receipt is the file, not the chat. The chat says what happened; the file is what happened.

data.source: anthropic.com, 2026-09-22; OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra page is in the description

lines.text: Now the uncomfortable part. The labs publish how often their agents finish tasks on a real computer, on a benchmark called OSWorld.
Anthropic reports 81.8 percent for Claude Opus 5.5, with partial credit. Read it the other way: about one task in five is not fully done.
For GPT-6 Astra, OpenAI's own launch page is linked in the description. Read its computer-use claim there and compare.

data.title: Four ways a task goes wrong

lines.text: When a task fails, it fails in one of four shapes.
It reads the wrong page, or stale data.
It finishes half the job and reports it as done.
It produces a confident wrong number.
Or it does something you never asked for, which is the shape that made the news last week.

scenes.chapter: Always-on: what the labs are building next

data.title: What changes when it never logs off
items: It acts while you are away
It runs in the background under the operating system's control, NVIDIA says of the new Windows agent framework
A persistent OpenAI assistant: reported, not announced, as we record

lines.text: Now the next step everyone is building: agents that keep working after you close the window.
It acts while you are away, so nobody is watching the loop.
It keeps state across chats, so a mistake in Monday's task can shape Friday's.
NVIDIA says the new Windows agent framework, part of its work with Microsoft, runs such agents in the background, under the operating system's control.
OpenAI is widely reported to be building a persistent assistant of its own. As we record, that is a report, not an announcement.
Whatever ships, the shape is the same: goal, tools, loop, and now a loop with no one in the room.

data.title: The three walls that keep an agent in its box

lines.text: If that worries you, good. Last video was about the three walls that keep an agent in its box: tools, network, secrets. Watch it next.

scenes.chapter: Three questions before you hand it a task

steps.title: What is the evidence?
steps.detail: A file, a diff, a booking reference. Not a summary

steps.title: What can it touch?
steps.detail: Tools, sites and secrets in reach while you are away

steps.title: What does a wrong answer cost?
steps.detail: Cheap to check, or expensive to undo?

lines.text: So here are the three questions to ask before you hand an agent a task.
One, what evidence will I get that it finished? A file, a diff, a booking reference. A summary is not evidence.
Two, what can it touch while I am not watching? Tools, sites, secrets. If the answer is everything, stop.
Three, what does a wrong answer cost me? A blank cell is cheap. A wrong booking or a deleted folder is not.

messages.name: Bad ask
messages.text: Book me a table for Friday.

messages.name: Good ask
messages.text: List three options. Don't book anything.

lines.text: Same errand, two ways to ask.
Book me a table for Friday hands over money and a decision, with no evidence until the confirmation lands.
List three options and do not book anything gives you a checkable list, and keeps the decision with you.

scenes.chapter: So is the chatbot really over?

data.title: The chat is now the receipt
data.cta: Read the file, not the summary.
lines: Ask for evidence, limit reach, price the mistake
Next: which AI is actually worth paying for

lines.text: So is the chatbot over? Not quite. The chat is now the receipt, and the work happens behind it.
Your job changed too: from asking good questions to setting good boundaries, and reading the file, not the summary.
Next time, we start from the prices this agent found and I will show you which model is actually worth paying for.
